binders: fp is an abstract arithmetic package consisting of a standard floating-addition model, an exact two-component addition operation tied to that model, and an exact two-component product operation.
n and K are natural numbers.
x and y are real vectors indexed by Fin(n+1), equivalently x=(x_0,…,x_n) and y=(y_0,…,y_n).
hypotheses: Writing u for the real parameter extracted from fp, the package entails u≥0, fl(0,a)=a, and for every a,b there exists a δ depending on a,b such that |δ|≤u and fl(a,b)=(a+b)(1+δ).
If twoSum(a,b)=(s,e), then s=fl(a,b), s+e=a+b, and |e|≤u|s|. If twoProduct(a,b)=(p,q), then p+q=ab and |q|≤u|ab|.
8(n+1)u≤1, where n+1 is interpreted as a real in this inequality.
conclusions: Let C be the computed quantity defined below, d=Σ_{i=0}^n x_i y_i, A=Σ_{i=0}^n |x_i||y_i|, and g=((4n+2)u)/(1-(4n+2)u). Then |C-d|≤(u+2g²)|d|+g^K A.
mathematical_definitions: For any nonempty real vector v=(v_0,…,v_{m-1}), define its transform T(v) as follows. Set s_0=v_0; for j=0,…,m-2 let twoSum(s_j,v_{j+1})=(s_{j+1},e_j); then T(v)=(e_0,…,e_{m-2},s_{m-1}). For m=1 this gives T(v)=(v_0).
Define F to be the recursive floating sum using fl: F of an empty vector is 0, F(v_0)=v_0, and for m≥2, F(v_0,…,v_{m-1})=fl(F(v_0,…,v_{m-2}),v_{m-1}).
For each i=0,…,n, write twoProduct(x_i,y_i)=(p_i,q_i). Define the length-2(n+1) vector z=(q_0,…,q_n) concatenated with T(p_0,…,p_n).
For a nonnegative integer r, T^r denotes r repeated applications of T, with T^0 the identity.
Because K≥3, the computed quantity LocalDef005 fp K x y is exactly C=F(T^(K-2)(z)).
The exact dot product is d=Σ_{i=0}^n x_i y_i, and the componentwise absolute-product sum is A=Σ_{i=0}^n |x_i||y_i|.
The natural expression 4(n+1)-2 uses truncated natural subtraction but equals 4n+2. Thus g=LocalDef008(u,4(n+1)-2)=((4n+2)u)/(1-(4n+2)u).
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every abstract arithmetic package satisfying the stated floating-addition, exact two-sum, and exact two-product models, every pair of real vectors of length n+1, and every K≥3 satisfying 8(n+1)u≤1, form all product residuals, apply one exact sum-preserving transform to the product principal components, concatenate those two blocks, apply K-2 further exact sum-preserving transforms, and finally left-sum the resulting vector with the modeled floating addition. The absolute difference between that computed real number and the exact dot product is at most (u+2g²) times the absolute exact dot product plus g^K times the sum of the componentwise absolute products, where g=((4n+2)u)/(1-(4n+2)u).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The dimension parameter n may be zero, but the input vectors still have length n+1, so the actual input dimension is always at least one.
The theorem asserts a result only when K≥3. For a particular K<3, the proof-valued hypothesis is unavailable and the corresponding implication is vacuous.
The theorem asserts a result only when 8(n+1)u≤1. For package and dimension choices violating this condition, the corresponding implication is vacuous.
The nested package structure encodes u≥0, so the smallness condition cannot be satisfied merely by choosing a negative u.
Under u≥0 and 8(n+1)u≤1, (4n+2)u<1, so the denominator 1-(4n+2)u is positive and the definition of g is nonsingular.
Natural subtraction is truncated in the definitions. The target hypotheses ensure the algorithmic count (K-1)-1 equals K-2, while 4(n+1)-2 equals 4n+2 for every natural n.
There are no restrictions on signs, zeros, magnitudes, ordering, conditioning, or nonvanishing of the entries of x and y or of their dot product.
The error is an absolute scalar error. The proposition does not state a relative-error bound when the exact dot product is nonzero.

All values are mathematical reals and all finite sums outside the abstract fl, twoSum, and twoProduct operations are exact. Overflow, underflow, subnormal behavior, representability, and a concrete rounding mode are not encoded.
The first component of twoProduct is constrained only through p+q=ab and |q|≤u|ab|; no separate rounded-multiplication operation or equation is specified.
Each relative-error witness δ for fl may depend independently on its two operands; the proposition does not assert one common δ across all additions.
The proposition gives this upper bound but does not encode sharpness, attainability, or a lower bound on the error.
